Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Dylan Johnson, Assistant SecretaryBureau of Global Public Affairs

Via Teleconference

Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Venezuela

Remarks

October 26, 2026

ASSISTANT SECRETARY JOHNSON:  To ask a question, please use the “raise your hand” feature.  And then once you’re called on, you’ll have to unmute your phone to ask your question.  And we will give it a second for people to call in here.  Okay.  We will start with Gabe Gutierrez of NBC.

QUESTION:  Thank you, Mr. Secretary.  I appreciate you doing this.  With the timing of María Corina Machado’s return, can you say if the U.S. either urged her to return at this time – did it in any way facilitate her return?  And then also more of a – on a housekeeping question, how much oil has the U.S. brought in from Venezuela to date since Maduro’s arrest?  I know the President has given various numbers, but what is the most updated figure you have on how much oil has come to –

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I – yeah, on the oil, I don’t have an updated figure.  I mean, what happens is Venezuela is now selling the oil on the global market.  Some of it – a lot of it is heavy crude is refined in our refineries in the – in the southern U.S.  Some of it is refined in India, which is increasing its intake of it.  But it’s basic – here’s what happened before.  Venezuelan oil, because it was sanctioned, had to be sold basically at a discount.  The Chinese never paid for Venezuelan oil.  They would basically take $100 worth of oil and, instead of paying for it in cash, would just credit it against the debt that Venezuela owed them. 

In other cases, they had to sell it at deep discounts around the world because of the – what happened after January 3rd was the oil is now being sold at market rate, deposited into the Treasury-controlled account, and then that money is paid on a monthly and biweekly basis via a process that’s been created and placed with the licenses through Treasury.  But I don’t know the exact amount that’s been processed through that account.  I just don’t know.  I mean, energy – I can get you the answer.  I just don’t have it in front of me. 

On the first part of your question, with María Corina, look, the only time I ever discouraged her, for example – me personally – from going, was right after the earthquake.  And the reason why was very simple, because right – at that moment the only thing we were focused on, from a logistical standpoint, was getting as many planes with relief aid as possible into the country.  And I said to her right now the only thing we’re focused on – at one point we were running the airport there – is making sure that we can get aid into the country. 

So, that’s the only time I said it’s probably not the best time to return, in the midst of a humanitarian calamity, because of the fact that we wanted to make sure that we were getting the planes in there and that the planes were filled, that there would be no impediments to the planes landing or things of this nature.  Because all we wanted to do was get first responders and aid into the country as quickly as possible, because they were facing a very real calamity, which it was.  It’s probably the worst earthquake of this hemisphere in 50 years, if not longer. 

On the issue of what happened yesterday, I – we’re well aware that she wanted to go back.  And the only thing I can tell you about “facilitate” is weeks ago – and I mean weeks and weeks ago – we spoke to the interim authorities and just said, look, our expectation is that she’s a Venezuelan, she belongs in her country.  That’s the country she’s from.  She should be allowed to return, and she should be allowed to return unperturbed, having no problems.  And they told us that she could fly into the airport if she wanted to, and we communicated that to her team. 

So she chose to – now, I think she’s had some impediments according to them, but that had nothing to do with us.  Those were bilateral impediments.  Those were countries that didn’t want to be seen – that have their own interests when it comes to Venezuela, for example, and countries that didn’t want to be getting crossways for one reason or another.  But from our perspective, weeks and weeks ago they told us that she could go back and she would not be disturbed.  And my understanding is when she entered yesterday, and she’s gone through the country, and she had no issues and no problems – no problems getting in and no problems once she’s been in.

ASSISTANT SECRETARY JOHNSON:  Great.  We’ll take our next question from Ed Wong of The New York Times.

I think you’re on mute, Ed.  Hello? 

QUESTION:  Oh, hi.  Okay.  I unmuted.  Secretary –

SECRETARY RUBIO:  You almost lost your turn.  You almost lost your turn; you’re lucky.  Go ahead. 

QUESTION:  Thanks; appreciate it.  So I wanted to ask about a tension that exists in statements that María Corina has made about the current oil deal.  She’s criticized Betancourt.  I know that the U.S. sees this oil deal as the best chance for Venezuela to bolster its economy and get revenue into the country.  Machado herself has criticized it; she might do that again in the future.  She says Betancourt represents the old regime and the oligarchy associated with that.  So how do you address that?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, first of all, you have to understand the oil deal – the oil deal is just a portion of the overall industry there.  This company, NABEP, this blue – whatever, Blue Energy – they control the oil fields that, many of them, the majority of the oil fields they controlled were once being processed or held by Chinese or Russian companies.  So we could’ve left it that way, I guess.  Or we can decide to enter into this strategic agreement with this company.  They’re the single largest private company operating under license in Venezuela, but they are not the totality of Venezuela’s oil industry.  There’s plenty of other fields, including the ones Chevron has expanded into, including the ones Exxon is interested in, including the ones that Reliance is interested in, from India. 

So it’s – and the deal – what the deal does do, okay, from – is because of the U.S. Government’s involvement, is it now allows the company that we partnered with to go out and make massive capital investments to increase the productive capacity.  Understand that because of sanctions and corruption, there’s been very little investment in the capital, in the infrastructure of their energy sector.  So they’re underproducing, and a lot of this – they didn’t invest anything in capital.  Right, the kleptocracy just stole all the money from it but didn’t really invest anything back in the business. 

The fact that they’re in business with us, the fact that they are now partnered with the United States, gives the certainty they need, and they’ve already started doing it, to go out and make massive investments in capital – which they’re doing.  Not a penny’s coming from us.  We’re not putting a dollar into this.  But it’s created the market confidence that they can now go out and raise the money to bring in the capital investment to increase the productive capacity of Venezuela.

The second thing is it speaks to the United States a huge strategic advantage, which is it gives us access to basically a reserve that, in times of crisis or need, we would have access to.  Otherwise, it generates revenue, all of which would have to pay royalties to the government.

As far as her criticism of the deal, I mean, that’s fine.  I mean, that’s her opinion on it.  And eventually – this is a contract that we think is a very solid contract.  It’ll ultimately – it’s a deal that is going to have to comply with all the American laws on money laundering and corruption and the U.S. courts and things of that nature.  So we feel it’s a very, very solid deal.  She doesn’t have to agree with it or like it, but I think that’s separate from the issue of having an election and a democracy. 

I think no matter what, once people understand what the deal means, it’s just a portion of the overall energy sector in Venezuela.  And whether it was us or the Chinese or the Russians, someone was going to be in business with these people because these are productive fields.  So, we think they’re better off being in business with us than somebody else, and it just allows them to be able to quickly invest in the capital necessary to increase the productive capacity of a country that’s been severely underinvested in.

QUESTION:  All right.  I think I learned how to work this.  Can you hear me?

ASSISTANT SECRETARY JOHNSON:  We got you.

QUESTION:  All right, excellent.  How on the level do you think Delcy Rodríguez is here?  You’re going to be asking her to essentially give up power a few years early.  And then a more micro note, today in her press conference in Caracas, she twice denounced the, quote, “external aggression,” the military-style aggression against Venezuela, clearly referring to the United States.  So I’m curious what our trust is – what your trust is – in her. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, three things.  Number one, your Miami Hurricanes were very vulnerable to Hail Mary passes, just so you know.  Number two, as you’ve witnessed the last two weeks, this – I shouldn’t be bragging because the Gators kind of had a couple bad weeks, Marc. 

All right, let me go back to your question on Delcy.  Yeah, I don’t think Delcy’s ever pronounced herself in favor of the operation that happened on January 3rd.  That said, so far this process – how do we judge all this?  We ultimately judge it not by rhetoric but by action, okay?  And the actions are as follows:  We have asked them to do certain things that are in the interest of the national security of the United States, and they have done them – some of which I’m not going to disclose or talk about here, but they’ve done them.  I can – suffice it to say that today the influence of Iranians and Cubans in Venezuela is – and others is substantially diminished, if not eliminated. 

They’ve – we’ve asked them to go after criminal organizations, and they’ve done it.  We’ve asked them to deport individuals wanted by the justice system of the United States, like Alex Saab, and they’ve extradited him, and today he’s pled guilty and is now a cooperating witness in our system.  We’ve asked them to make sure that this transition process moves forward, and they’re doing it.  I mean, these agreements, they’ve agreed to them.  They’ve agreed to the new TSJ.  They’ve agreed to this moving forward. 

So, I think the question about trust – look, trust is – it’s not based on rhetoric.  It’s going to be based on actions.  At the end of the day, that’s really what we care about.  If at the end of the day we have a new TSJ, a new CNE, a new election, and a new system of government, that’s what we want.  And no matter what people say along the way, as long as it happens, this is a results-based process.  And so far, frankly, on everything we’ve asked for in this process, be it the economic reforms, the political reforms, it’s happening.  And we think that’s good and that’s cooperative, irrespective of the other things that are happening.

The second thing I would say about the – I think your question was about – what was the other part of your question? 

Did we mute him?  What happened?

ASSISTANT SECRETARY JOHNSON:  Can we unmute Marc again, guys?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I think that covered the gist of what he was asking about, right?

ASSISTANT SECRETARY JOHNSON:  Okay.  We’ll now go to The Wall Street Journal.  We’ll do Vera Bergengruen.

QUESTION:  All right, can you hear me now?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.

QUESTION:  Okay.  Thank you for laying this out.  So, you’ve laid out all these conditions that need to be met, obviously, before Venezuela can hold elections.  But what prevents the current government from – it’s a lot, and obviously, as you said, it takes a really long time for all of this to kind of fall into place.  What prevents the current government from using these requirements to delay elections indefinitely?  And how would Washington use its leverage, as you’ve mentioned, to prevent that?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I mean, what prevents them from doing it is the fact that – let me put it to you this way.  I think your question really is, well, how do we know that this is not a delay tactic?  Like, what if they just try to wait us out for two years?  That’s not going to happen.  I mean, we have timelines that are agreed to, and so far, they’ve met every one of the timelines.  And I say that despite the delay that happened with the earthquake sort of slowing down some of this. 

But, I mean, we have very clear expectations, and at the end of the day, Venezuela is still an economy and a country that operates on sanctions, that is still heavily sanctioned.  And to the extent they’re able to do business and operate today, it is because we are issuing waivers or general licenses that are allowing certain economic activities to happen.  So, the truth be told is the United States has significant influence over the direction that these talks go and the results that we get from them.  So, our expectation, I don’t – look, I don’t want to be hostile here because so far they’ve – everything we’ve asked them to do, they’ve done, and they’ve met all the timelines that we’re working on.

If that process doesn’t work out, then we’re back to where we were from the beginning, I suppose, but that’s why this process has to work.  And that’s why we don’t want to see – that’s why I made a very clear reference to it yesterday, and that is that everybody should be committed  to this process of transition – everybody.  That includes the interim authorities.  And I have no indication that they do not intend to cooperate with this process that we’ve laid out in terms of how this needs to transition.  I don’t know what choice they have because if they don’t cooperate with it, obviously, the United – then it’s the reason why we’ve suspended some of these sanctions.  It’s the reason why we’ve allowed certain economic activities to occur.  It’s the reason why we’ve done a bunch of the things we’ve done, as an incentive to continue this process moving forward.

But I’m hopeful that they will continue to meet these expectations because, frankly, it’s in their best interest in the long term as well.  But, I mean, we’re not going to get – no one’s going to wait us out here.  I mean, I recognize the calendar and the time frame and the constraints.  I mean, best-case scenario, I’m in this job for two more years and two months.  So, I clearly intend to see this thing well in advance of the time I leave this position, or positions.  So we’re very committed to that, and I feel very optimistic that we’re going to meet those timelines and bring us to where we need to be.

ASSISTANT SECRETARY JOHNSON:  All right.  And we’ll take our last question from Olivia Gazis of CBS.  I think you’re on mute.

QUESTION:  Can you hear me?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yes.

ASSISTANT SECRETARY JOHNSON:  We got you.

QUESTION:  Okay, thank you.  Thank you, Mr. Secretary.  Just to drill down on what you’ve just said, in addition to the asks and expectations, have Delcy and Jorge been offered any incentives by the U.S. to facilitate a transition, including immunity from prosecution? 

And if I may, since it’s the last call, on Cuba and the messaging there where you’re also pushing for political change, why are you urging the Cubans to work with the CIA rather than organize peacefully?  What are you asking them to do?  Thank you.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, I’m not going to answer the second question, unfortunately.  I’m just – I can’t answer that other than to say that we think Cuba needs very dramatic change, and the direction – I mean, it’s a totally different case from Venezuela, looks very different.  And I’ll leave it at that, unfortunately, on the second point.

On your first point, no, there’s definitely no talk about prosecutions or anything of this nature.  It’s very simple, okay?  Venezuela has two choices.  There’s only two choices right now for Venezuela, and I would say this is true for everybody involved, okay?  I’m not just speaking now about Delcy and Jorge or any of these other people on the – in the interim government, and I’m not speaking about the opposition.  I’m just speaking for everybody.  Venezuela has two options here. 

Option one is to truly enter into a period of both reconciliation and reformation so that they can have elections that result not just in a democratically elected government but an enduring republic.  And that gives them the opportunity to prosper economically and be a country that, once again, is a place where the economy’s prospering, the people are happy, and 7 million people don’t have to flee, and many of them can actually come back and live in their country again.  That’s option A.  And the only process that gets us there is the process we are on right now.  Okay? 

I witnessed for 15 years and I supported all of these movements – the street protests, the marches, the taking on the water cannons, the political prisoners going in, the sanctioning – all of that.  I mean, this – I’ve been involved in this issue of Venezuela since 2014, so I’ve watched every iteration of it: the failed attempt in the Trump 1 administration to get an internal rebellion.  By the way, that was supposed to be led by the head of the transitional – of the TSJ at that – Maikel Moreno at the time, that ended up not working.  I’ve watched all of these things move forward.  And you’re not going to street-protest your way into a democracy.  It’s just not – the way you do it peacefully is through a process, and it’s the one we’ve set up.  And if this process doesn’t work, then the alternative is going to be worse.  The alternative is going to be either violence and armed conflict within the country, or back to the way things have been for the last 20 years, which have not been good for the people of Venezuela. 

So from our point of view, whether – this is the only process, it’s the only game in town.  This process has to work.  And if it – and if it fails, then I think – guys, in the end, my interest here is ensuring that Venezuela can have a functioning republic with a system of laws where there’s an opposition but there’s also a majority party; people every four years go vote, or five years, or three years, whatever they decide – they go vote for a new National Assembly, for new presidents, they change back and forth, like it is in multiple countries throughout the region; and an economy that has an opportunity to succeed so that not only do the people that live there now be able to continue to live there, but 6 or 7 million people that were forced to flee the country will be able to go back to their country.  A lot of them want to go back and be in Venezuela again, and they’re scattered all over the world.  And I want all that to happen without bloodshed.  I want all that to happen without civil war.  I want all that to happen without getting back into an endless cycle of sanctions and threats and back and forth.  And we’re trying to give that process a chance to work, and this is the closest we’ve ever been. 

And the difference between this process and what the Biden administration negotiated is they made a bunch of front-end concessions that were irreversible – we’ve made no irreversible concessions – and they allowed the elections to move forward using the current infrastructure, which was designed by the Maduro regime to rig elections.  So, that infrastructure has to be replaced in order for these elections to be valid.  How can you have a legitimate election in Venezuela when the Electoral Council is controlled by people loyal to one side, with the power to decide that certain so-and-so can’t run for election, so they can’t be on the ballot?  How can you have a legitimate election in Venezuela when you have a supreme court that is fully politicized and is going to rule that anything the regime wants is legal and allowed to do?  You’ve got to change the infrastructure of the elections – not in 10 years, not in five years, not in two years; it needs to happen quickly under the timelines that we’ve established.  And I think we’re making real progress in that regard.  But if anybody tries to derail that process, they’re doing great harm to Venezuela, who no matter – if that’s the interim authorities that try to do harm to this process or stop complying, then we’re going to have a problem.  But I don’t expect that.  I really, really don’t.  But, like I said, we’re going to be on top of it because it’s a priority.

ASSISTANT SECRETARY JOHNSON:  All right, thank you, Mr. Secretary, and thanks to everyone for dialing in.  If you have any additional questions regarding today’s call, you can send them to the Department’s media inquiry system at state.gov/newsroom.  Thank you.  This concludes today’s call.

ASSISTANT SECRETARY JOHNSON:  Can we unmute Marc again, guys?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I think that covered the gist of what he was asking about, right?

ASSISTANT SECRETARY JOHNSON:  Okay.  We’ll now go to The Wall Street Journal.  We’ll do Vera Bergengruen.

QUESTION:  All right, can you hear me now?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.

QUESTION:  Okay.  Thank you for laying this out.  So, you’ve laid out all these conditions that need to be met, obviously, before Venezuela can hold elections.  But what prevents the current government from – it’s a lot, and obviously, as you said, it takes a really long time for all of this to kind of fall into place.  What prevents the current government from using these requirements to delay elections indefinitely?  And how would Washington use its leverage, as you’ve mentioned, to prevent that?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I mean, what prevents them from doing it is the fact that – let me put it to you this way.  I think your question really is, well, how do we know that this is not a delay tactic?  Like, what if they just try to wait us out for two years?  That’s not going to happen.  I mean, we have timelines that are agreed to, and so far, they’ve met every one of the timelines.  And I say that despite the delay that happened with the earthquake sort of slowing down some of this. 

But, I mean, we have very clear expectations, and at the end of the day, Venezuela is still an economy and a country that operates on sanctions, that is still heavily sanctioned.  And to the extent they’re able to do business and operate today, it is because we are issuing waivers or general licenses that are allowing certain economic activities to happen.  So, the truth be told is the United States has significant influence over the direction that these talks go and the results that we get from them.  So, our expectation, I don’t – look, I don’t want to be hostile here because so far they’ve – everything we’ve asked them to do, they’ve done, and they’ve met all the timelines that we’re working on.

But I’m hopeful that they will continue to meet these expectations because, frankly, it’s in their best interest in the long term as well.  But, I mean, we’re not going to get – no one’s going to wait us out here.  I mean, I recognize the calendar and the time frame and the constraints.  I mean, best-case scenario, I’m in this job for two more years and two months.  So, I clearly intend to see this thing well in advance of the time I leave this position, or positions.  So we’re very committed to that, and I feel very optimistic that we’re going to meet those timelines and bring us to where we need to be.

ASSISTANT SECRETARY JOHNSON:  All right.  And we’ll take our last question from Olivia Gazis of CBS.  I think you’re on mute.

QUESTION:  Can you hear me?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yes.

ASSISTANT SECRETARY JOHNSON:  We got you.

So from our point of view, whether – this is the only process, it’s the only game in town.  This process has to work.  And if it – and if it fails, then I think – guys, in the end, my interest here is ensuring that Venezuela can have a functioning republic with a system of laws where there’s an opposition but there’s also a majority party; people every four years go vote, or five years, or three years, whatever they decide – they go vote for a new National Assembly, for new presidents, they change back and forth, like it is in multiple countries throughout the region; and an economy that has an opportunity to succeed so that not only do the people that live there now be able to continue to live there, but 6 or 7 million people that were forced to flee the country will be able to go back to their country.  A lot of them want to go back and be in Venezuela again, and they’re scattered all over the world.  And I want all that to happen without bloodshed.  I want all that to happen without civil war.  I want all that to happen without getting back into an endless cycle of sanctions and threats and back and forth.  And we’re trying to give that process a chance to work, and this is the closest we’ve ever been.

item.title: Joint Statement on Famine in Sudan
item.dc:creator: Office of the Spokesman
item.description:
Office of the Spokesman

Joint Statement on Famine in Sudan

Media Note

October 26, 2026

The text of the following statement was released by the European Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management, and the Governments of Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Croatia, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Hungary, Latvia, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland,Portugal, Romania, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, the United States of America and the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

Begin text.

Sudan is experiencing an alarming deterioration in its food security. The risk of famine in the coming months, as warned by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, needs urgent action. There is no time to lose to save lives and prevent famine.

An estimated 19.5 million people (41% of the country’s population) are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, including 5 million facing emergency levels of food insecurity. Without immediate action to reverse the current trajectory, the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000. The number of food insecure areas, initially assessed at 14, is expected to double.

Conflict is the key driver of Sudan’s hunger crisis, displacing millions of people, damaging critical infrastructure and disrupting healthcare provision, food production, supply chains and markets. The situation is being exacerbated by systematic obstruction of aid and the effects of El Niño, which has resulted in reduced rainfall and increased drought across over half of Sudan.

The parties to the conflict bear primary responsibility for alleviating the suffering of the Sudanese people. We urge the parties to lift all impediments on humanitarian assistance, allow and facilitate full, safe, rapid, and unimpeded humanitarian access, and protect humanitarian personnel. Left unchecked, these impediments will hamper the ability of the humanitarian response to address famine risk. In practice, we call on the parties to:

  • Authorise humanitarian operations through all crossline and cross-border routes, including air access into Darfur which will allow for the rapid deployment of aid operations and timely aid worker medical evacuations;
  • Sustain presence and protection of humanitarian personnel throughout Sudan, including reducing delays for visas and customs clearance, increasing the duration of visas and travel permits and removing additional permits, taxations and other bureaucratic requirements slowing aid delivery;
  • Refrain from strikes on civilian infrastructure, including agriculture and food systems, which are critical to the delivery of essential services to the civilian population.
  • Strengthen civil-military coordination to ensure the safety of humanitarians and humanitarian sites.

In the face of a potential famine, we call on all members of the international community to urgently scale up funding in response to increased needs and support efforts to ensure assistance reaches those most in need. We further encourage development and financial institutions to adapt their ongoing programmes to the food security situation and focus on the areas of greatest need. Together we must act without delay to avert famine by supporting the winter cropping season and strengthening locally led responses.

We stand with the people of Sudan and humanitarian organisations who are working tirelessly and under extremely challenging conditions to provide life-saving assistance.

item.title: Joint Communiqué from U.S.–Pacific Islands Conference of Police Ministers
item.dc:creator: Office of the Spokesman
item.description:
Office of the Spokesman

Joint Communiqué from U.S.–Pacific Islands Conference of Police Ministers

Media Note

October 26, 2026

Begin Text

Securing the Pacific Together

1.The United States and Palau hosted partners responsible for police matters, including ministers and senior law enforcement leaders of Australia, the Cook Islands, Ecuador, Fiji, France together with New Caledonia and French Polynesia, Kiribati, the Republic of the Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, Naoero, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Samoa, Tonga, Tuvalu, and Vanuatu. Representatives of the Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat and PACPOL Secretariat also attended. The inaugural U.S.–Pacific Islands Conference of Police Ministers (COPMIN) gathered in Los Angeles, California, on October 21 and 22, 2026, to address security challenges and affirm our intentions to address them to better secure the Pacific together.

I. Shared Vision

2. As Pacific countries, territories, and partners working together in the region, we recognize our shared interest in a safe and secure Blue Pacific Continent. The safety, security and prosperity of our communities are central to this shared interest. Transnational criminal networks exploit our interconnected waters, borders and economies, requiring coordinated action and strong partnerships. COPMIN has provided an opportunity for Pacific countries, together with regional and international partners, to strengthen cooperation against these common threats. In pursuing these shared objectives, we reaffirm the central role of the Pacific Islands Forum in setting regional peace and security priorities, and the role of the Pacific Police Ministers Meeting in guiding regional policing efforts. Our work in the Pacific will respect national sovereignty and align with these priorities, including those set out in the Forum’s Pacific Regional Peace and Security Action Plan 2026–2030, particularly on transnational organized crime and drugs

II. Maritime Security and Supply Chains

3. Methamphetamine, cocaine, and other synthetic drugs are reaching our communities in unprecedented quantities. We note that, since 2024, narcotics trafficked by Western Hemisphere cartels through the Pacific have surpassed those originating from Asia and that semi-submersible vessels used by cartels have been recovered in Fiji, the Marshall Islands, and Solomon Islands waters. These communities bear the cost in addiction, in violence, and in the corrosion of institutions.

4. Our law enforcement services have seized record quantities of cartel-linked cocaine in the past year, in operations built on information shared across borders and on trusted partnerships our officers have cultivated over years. We commend the leadership of Pacific police and the coordinated efforts of customs, immigration, maritime authorities, regional agencies and international partners in securing these outcomes.

5. We commit to strengthening maritime and border capabilities to disrupt drug trafficking and other transnational organized crime. This includes, in accordance with national laws, capacities, and consent, enhancing maritime domain awareness, and, where applicable, utilizing maritime law enforcement agreements, letters of agreement for foreign assistance, and Shiprider cooperation with the United States; strengthening port and border security; and detecting and halting illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing, particularly by transnational organized crime groups.

6. We recognize the contribution of health, education, and social service agencies, together with civil society and communities in addressing the impacts of illicit drugs. We support community-based, faith-based, and evidence-based approaches to preventing drug-related harm, disrupting criminal recruitment and reducing demand for illicit drugs, and we support access to treatment, rehabilitation and reintegration, including in remote and outer island communities, consistent with our national and regional strategies and building on the outcomes of relevant regional meetings.

7. We further commit to strengthening cross-regional information sharing on trafficking routes, criminal networks, and maritime logistics in coordination with existing national and regional arrangements, consistent with national laws and agreed priorities. We welcome the cross-regional exchange convened at COPMIN with partners from Ecuador and the Philippines, and we will continue to build on these connections to advance our shared peace and security goals.

8. We will strengthen the integrity of legitimate supply chains to prevent their exploitation by criminal networks, disrupt the flow of illicit drugs, and support secure and efficient trade. We will also target the supply of precursor chemicals, equipment and materials used in illicit drug manufacture, using the full range of regulatory, enforcement and legal measures available.

III. Cyber-Enabled Crime and Illicit Finance

9. Online scam operations target our citizens on an industrial scale. Criminal networks build and operate the compounds, platforms, and infrastructure behind cyber-enabled fraud; recruit, coerce, and traffic victims across borders; and move the proceeds of these crimes through formal and informal financial channels across jurisdictions.

10. We will increase information sharing on scam operations, criminal infrastructure, and cryptocurrency laundering, consistent with national laws, and to build the capacity of our national cyber authorities, law enforcement agencies and financial intelligence units, including those of small island states, to disrupt, detect, investigate, and prosecute these crimes as well as the corrupt officials that allow criminal networks to operate with impunity. We will work together to strengthen and implement anti-money laundering and cybercrime frameworks, consistent with national laws and capacities and supported by technical assistance where needed, and to protect Pacific access to the global financial system, in line with the Pacific Islands Forum Regional Peace and Security Action Plan 2026-2030.

11. We recognize the contributions of industry partners represented at COPMIN, and we welcome continued engagement with trusted technology providers on maritime domain awareness, financial-crime analytics, and secure digital infrastructure, consistent with national laws, procurement requirements and data governance arrangements.

IV. Results

12. We welcome the following:

  • The United States’ initiative to establish a cross-regional information-sharing mechanism connecting the Pacific Islands with the Americas and maritime Southeast Asia. This is to be developed in consultation with participants and in coordination with existing regional bodies and arrangements, including under the Forum’s Pacific Regional Peace and Security Action Plan 2026–2030.
  • The United States’ announcement of investments to strengthen law enforcement cooperation, counter drug trafficking, and combat transnational crime, in consultation with recipient governments and in coordination with regional arrangements.

13. We commit to continuing and strengthening our enduring efforts to secure our shared Pacific region, and to work together to identify resourcing that will sustain this work.

V. Status Of This Communiqué

14. This Communiqué is a statement of shared intent and is not legally binding. Forum Members will report on the outcomes of COPMIN to the Pacific Islands Forum through the relevant regional security processes.

VI. Closing Affirmation

15. We, the participants in COPMIN, commit to fighting transnational crime and strengthening maritime security in the Blue Pacific Continent to better protect all our communities from the evolving threats of today and the future.

End Text

item.title: Senior State Department Official on Venezuela
item.dc:creator: Senior State Department Official
item.description:
Senior State Department Official

Via Teleconference

Senior State Department Official on Venezuela

Remarks

October 26, 2026

MODERATOR:  Hey guys, good afternoon.  Thank you for joining today’s press call on Venezuela.  Just to start with the ground rules, this call will be held on background attributable to a Senior State Department Official.  That’s on background attributable to a Senior State Department Official.  And with that I would introduce our speaker, , for remarks.

SENIOR STATE DEPARTMENT OFFICIAL:  Okay, so the reason why I’m going to do it on background is because it’s extensive and highly technical in nature, so it just lays the groundwork.

I know a few of you traveled down for the fourth round of talks on the transition and reconciliation process in Venezuela, and it really hasn’t gotten nearly as much attention as some of the other more higher-profile things on the economic side, the oil deals and et cetera.  But I thought it was important to sort of lift the curtain a little bit and give you guys a view of exactly how we foresee this process playing out for the benefit of everyone involved.

So let me lay the groundwork.  Some of this is – for some of you, you probably know this because you’ve covered Venezuela over the years and Latin America in general.  For others this may be new, so I apologize if it’s redundant for some of you. 

But basically, like many of the countries in the Western Hemisphere that follow civil law and things of that nature, the courts are really the most powerful institution in many – especially for authoritarian regimes.  They use the courts as a way to basically declare anything legal or illegal that they want and to determine all kinds of things in the country. 

In the case of Venezuela, that is the Supreme Justice Tribunal, the TSJ as it’s called.  It has long been an instrument of the regime and Maduro, and 2015 really amped that up.  In fact, it was the TSJ that ruled that the National Assembly was illegal.  It was the TSJ that created the groundwork for a constituent assembly that replaced it with a new National Assembly.  It’s the TSJ that controls everything there.  So, it is the most powerful institution.  That’s the first thing to understand. 

The second thing is for elections in the country.  The elections in the country are run by the CNE, which is basically the Consejo Nacional Electoral, the National Electoral Council.  In Venezuela, that council isn’t just your elections department.  So, I live in county and they run the elections.  They put out the machines, they tabulate the votes.  This council theoretically does that, but it does much more than that.  It also decides which parties get to register and who gets to run.  And that’s how they disqualified María Corina, for example, and a bunch of other people, and Edmundo ended up being sort of like the default candidate because they forgot to remove him.

So, with that groundwork in place, let me go back in history a little bit as to why these efforts have failed in the past.  If you recall that under the Biden administration, they negotiated extensively with the Maduro regime on new elections in 2024, and they reached an agreement on new elections in 2024.  And as product of that agreement, the Biden administration gave the Maduro regime all kinds of concessions, including sanctions relief, but they also released the narcotrafficking convicted nephews of Cilia Maduro – Cilia, Maduro’s wife.  They released Alex Saab as part of that deal, all irreversible concessions that they made.

Venezuela and the Maduro regime then proceeded to have an election in 2024, but they had an election with the old TSJ, with the old CNE; in essence, with the existing infrastructure.  You cannot have a free and fair election that is accepted by both sides and all sides in a country as long as that infrastructure is in place.  So that infrastructure needs to be replaced.  That infrastructure needs to be ripped out and replaced with something new.  You can’t have credible elections in that country without that in place.

And so those are the steps that we are endeavoring to take here as regards to these talks.  So where are we right now on the talks?  Let’s talk about first the TSJ, which is the agreement they reached this week.  Both the opposition, the 2015 National Assembly, and the essence – in essence, representatives of the PSUV via Jorge Rodríguez, the party in power, have agreed – each have appointed members to a committee.  It is modeled judicial nominating committee, and that is a committee of people that will study candidates and nominate 32 people to become magistrates of the TSJ, the 32 magistrates of that process, through a JNC.

item.title: Secretary Rubio’s Travel to Atlanta to Host the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting
item.dc:creator: Office of the Spokesman
item.description:
Office of the Spokesman

Secretary Rubio’s Travel to Atlanta to Host the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting

Media Note

October 26, 2026

Secretary of State Marco Rubio will travel to Atlanta, Georgia from October 30–31 to host the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.  Under President Trump’s leadership, the United States is returning the G20 to its core economic mission of driving growth, strengthening economic security, and delivering results for the American people.

Secretary Rubio will convene foreign ministers from the world’s leading economies to advance practical cooperation on shared economic and security challenges.  As a global hub of diplomacy, connectivity, and commerce, Atlanta offers the perfect backdrop for these discussions.

Throughout the ministerial, the United States will work with G20 partners to address geopolitical crises contributing to global economic shocks, including threats to freedom of navigation, energy and food security, and supply chains.  Global security and economic prosperity are inextricably linked, and these discussions will set the stage for President Trump’s G20 Leaders’ Summit and the broader economic agenda that leaders will tackle.

Austria National Day

Press Statement

October 26, 2026

On behalf of the United States of America, I congratulate the people of Austria on your National Day. The United States and Austria have a long-standing relationship based on shared history, a commitment to freedom and sovereignty, and close ties between our citizens.

Austria is an important partner in Europe, and commercial ties are central to our relationship. Trade and investment between our countries continue to grow and support workers and businesses in both our nations. American and Austrian firms work together in energy, advanced technology, research, and innovation.

The United States wishes the people of Austria a successful year ahead, and we look forward to expanding our cooperation to bring greater security and prosperity to our citizens.

Kazakhstan Republic Day

Press Statement

October 24, 2026

On behalf of the United States of America, I extend congratulations to the government and people of Kazakhstan as they celebrate Republic Day on October 25th.

U.S.-Kazakhstan relations are at their strongest point in history as we celebrate 35 years of bilateral relations. Our countries are working together to strengthen regional security, expand economic cooperation, and create new commercial opportunities which will pair Kazakh ambition with American innovation to benefit both of our nations. We value Kazakhstan’s role as a diplomatic leader and strong supporter of President Trump’s peace initiatives. The United States looks forward to growing our partnership with Kazakhstan in the year ahead, both bilaterally and through our joint work in the C5+1 format.

October 24, 2026

On behalf of the United States of America, I extend congratulations to the government and people of Kazakhstan as they celebrate Republic Day on October 25th.

U.S.-Kazakhstan relations are at their strongest point in history as we celebrate 35 years of bilateral relations. Our countries are working together to strengthen regional security, expand economic cooperation, and create new commercial opportunities which will pair Kazakh ambition with American innovation to benefit both of our nations. We value Kazakhstan’s role as a diplomatic leader and strong supporter of President Trump’s peace initiatives. The United States looks forward to growing our partnership with Kazakhstan in the year ahead, both bilaterally and through our joint work in the C5+1 format.

Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Sergio Gor, U.S. Ambassador to India

Mumbai, India

Taj Mahal Palace Hotel

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor with Raj Chengappa of India Today

Interview

October 22, 2026

QUESTION:  Hello, I’m Raj Chengappa of India Today, and joining me for this very special conversation with this historic backdrop of the Gateway of India in Mumbai, are two of the most influential figures in India-U.S. relations: Secretary of State – U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor.  Thank you for joining us at India Today. 

And Ambassador, how would you rate India-U.S. relations?  If I give you a scale of one to 10, and 10 being the perfect partnership, how much would you put to that, and why?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I don’t put a number on it.  I wouldn’t put a number on it.  It’s a very important relationship, obviously; it’s two big, important countries.  We’ve worked together for a very long time.  We have a lot of common interests and we have a lot of – we have a history of working together.  And I think India is progressing so fast on so many areas that are important to the national security and national interest of the United States.  It’s a logical partnership. 

So, I don’t know about one to 10.  I would say it’s – I think it’s as strong as it’s ever been, and I think in five years we’ll look back and say it’s one of the strongest relationships in the world. 

QUESTION:  And two or three things that you think right now you are going to focus on?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, we’d like to get this trade agreement done, because I think that provides stability and certainty for everyone.  And then beyond that, I think there’s so many areas we can work on – on energy and certainly on technology like artificial intelligence and things of this nature, telecommunications.  There’s so much we can work on – biomedical, pharmaceuticals.  I mean, you name it.  I could go on for an hour. 

QUESTION:  All right.  Yes.

AMBASSADOR GOR:  And Raj, I’ll add to that that pick any sector, and today, the United States and India are working at it closer, at a higher level, and more engaged – whether that’s pharma, that’s military exercises.  India has more military exercises with the United States than anyone else.  So, any sector – IT, of course, sales, our bilateral trade – any sector, we’re working at it in a much higher level than ever before. 

QUESTION:  Well, it’s a bit humid.  I think let’s go inside and pursue this and get in depth, in the weeds of these questions.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  All right. 

AMBASASDOR GOR:  Absolutely.  Thank you.

QUESTION:  Come, come.  This is the historic Taj Mahal. 

(Break.)

QUESTION:  Secretary, continuing our conversation that we had, President Trump had said that India and the U.S. are pretty close to signing an agreement, and it will be different.  What I’d like to know:  Is Washington willing to give India the competitive tariff advantage it is seeking for this interim trade agreement? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I’m not going to get into the specifics of any agreement until they’re done, because there’s still a number of items being negotiated, although very few.  So, we’re very close, and I anticipate – I can’t – I can’t foresee anything that would keep us from reaching an agreement.  But there’s still some items that are being discussed.  So, I’d prefer not to go into the details of it until it’s all fully worked out. 

Suffice it to say that once this deal is done, it has to be one that’s beneficial to both countries.  And that’s what I anticipate it will be. 

QUESTION:  I think the concern is that India expects continuity rather than unpredictability, and there is a Super 301 provision hovering around.  So, could we expect that there will be continuity and not continuously have to revise our tariffs?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, that’s the point.  The point of having an agreement is to be able to have certainty so that people know they can invest, people know what the rules are that are going to govern trade and commerce between the two countries.  That’s the very purpose of having a deal.  And so that’s what we’re working towards, and I feel very optimistic that we’re going to get to a very good place very soon. 

QUESTION:  Excellent.  And Ambassador Gor, turning to you, when it comes to the investment relationship, where do you see the next big wave of American investment coming into India?  In which sectors do you think that will –

AMBASSADOR GOR:  Look, our bilateral trade is at an all-time high.  Our bilateral trade, 15 years ago it used to be to 20 billion.  Today it’s $240 billion.  And it goes both ways.  You have incredible investment coming into the United States.  The President recently hosted Essar in the Oval Office.  They’re opening incredible facilities, multibillion-dollar facilities in the United States that are creating jobs in local communities for Americans. 

On the other hand, this is a win-win situation.  We have American companies that have moved here, especially relating to IT.  Now, when they move here, that complements a job back home also.  This is not a one-way street.  And so our goal is to keep increasing that bilateral trade and identify those win-win situations. 

QUESTION:  Okay.  Moving to energy, Secretary Rubio, can you please elaborate on the national interest cited by President Trump for the U.S. to buy Russian diesel, and also a waiver of sanctions for India to buy Russian crude oil, when earlier we were actually penalized for doing this?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, a couple points.  The first is right now, you’re looking at global economy – all foreign policy has to be balanced.  Listen, you can’t just look at everything through the lens of one country or one conflict.  And right now, while we remain very concerned and we’re doing all we can to bring an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine, we also recognize the impact that that war is having on the global economy, in addition to what we’ve seen in the Straits of Hormuz and now increasingly the Red Sea.  And so, I think the President made a very wise decision, which is to, for some short period of time, allow there to be additional energy flows into the global marketplace, not just to benefit us – obviously it helps the United States – but also diesel prices are high all over the world. 

In the case of India, look, India has made real progress in diversifying its portfolio of energy.  And it’s done so not because of threats or anything of that nature.  It’s in India’s interest to diversify its portfolio, where it gets energy from.  You never want to be overly dependent on one country versus another.  So, it was already on that trajectory to begin with.  So, it’s not so much about buying less Russian oil than it is about buying more U.S. crude or Venezuelan or others from the Western Hemisphere.  I think that’s in India’s interests, and obviously we want to help facilitate it.  And more importantly, India’s real capability is the capability to ramp up refining, which crude oil is great, but you need to refine it in order for it to be a usable product.  And I think India has the capacity and the capability not just to refine more, but to, in very short order, have the kinds of investments that will allow it to expand its refining capability even further. 

QUESTION:  And that’s why you went to Jamnagar, and was it to enhance energy cooperation between India and the U.S.? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, we already have energy cooperation.  It’s more importantly to go see the facility and see how they’re operating and understand a little bit more about how it works.  It’s a very impressive facility.  But it also happens to be a company that has an investment in the United States, in Brownsville, that is hopefully going to be online by 2029.  So, it was a good opportunity to interact with a company that’s investing in expanding refining capability in the United States at the same time as a facility that I think can play a role in helping refine more crude from the Western Hemisphere and thereby allowing the world to diversify away from the Middle East. 

QUESTION:  I want to continue with this question of energy. 

AMBASSADOR GOR:  Yes.

QUESTION:  And if you look at India recently opening up its civil nuclear sector for private investment, particularly in the small modular reactors that we’re talking about, do you see now finally a breakthrough moment for American investment in technology in India? 

AMBASSADOR GOR:  We’ve had incredible momentum on that.  And as you know, things take time.  But to the government’s credit here, to Prime Minister Modi’s credit, the SHANTI bill passed, which enables SMRs and private technology and this new equipment to be able to come to India.  And so there has been some regulation challenges.  Nothing gets done overnight.  These are very complex issues, and they’ll set up the relationship for decades to come, right?  But India is one of the first places that the United States is looking at possibly to have our first SMRs internationally.  And so we’re on an incredible path there.  We’ve had meetings in Washington.  We’ve had meetings on this in Delhi.  We’ve had some meetings right here in Mumbai, because the regulatory agency for India is based here on that. 

So, it is moving in the right direction and I do think we’ll get there on that soon also. 

QUESTION:  Secretary, switching subjects, we are sitting inside the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel, which was, if you recall, the center of the horrific 26/11 terrorist attacks in India in 2008, and in fact you paid tribute to the victims of that.  What is America doing to assure India that its current closer ties with Pakistan will not come at the expense of India’s fight against terrorism? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, first of all, the United States has to have a relationship with as many countries in the world as possible because we have a global presence and a global interest in anything that’s going on.  So, our relationship with Pakistan is not new.  And I think it’s just developed in a way that allows us to have hopefully more influence over the decisions they make on a variety of topics.

In no way does the relationship with Pakistan come at the expense of our relationship with India.  We share the same concerns India does about terrorism.  We are not – we have been victims of terrorism, as India has been.  And we continue to – in fact, no country in the world does more to go after terrorism in the United States – than the United States.  It was the United States under President Trump that destroyed ISIS, or Daesh, in the Middle East.  It’s the United States that eroded al-Qaida.  It’s the United States that went in and eliminated bin Laden.  It’s the United States that’s gone in now and unfortunately has had to go into parts of Africa and take on these elements as well.

So, I don’t think any country in the world has shown a greater commitment to go after the terrorism – terrorism, global terrorism – than the United States has done, and that includes many of the same sort of ideologies that also threaten India. 

QUESTION:  And if you recall, last year you played quite a diplomatic role at Operation Sindoor after the terror attack in Pahalgam on that crucial day, on May 10th, I think, 2025, when you spoke directly to the leadership on both sides.  Could you take us behind the scenes of that particular thing?  And what, how did the conversation –

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I won’t take you behind the scenes because then no one will ever talk to me again in the future.  (Laughter.)  But no, so I can’t do that.  But I can just tell you, look, anytime we see a flashpoint between countries that could lead to a broader conflict and a war, if we can play a constructive role, we’ll try to.  And I think it’s a good example of our ability to speak to multiple parties and use – in the case of India a long pre-existing relationship, in the case of Pakistan one that I think has improved over the last few years – to just ensure that there isn’t flashpoints that could lead to something broader and more difficult. 

Look, the tensions that exist between the two countries are well understood.  I don’t need to sort of explain that to you or your audience.  But I can say to you with confidence that I think the United States is prepared to play a constructive role, because we’d prefer not to see war.  We’d prefer to see the opportunity to partner in business and commerce and do things that provide prosperity and security for the people of India, but also the people of the United States. 

QUESTION:  Right.  There have always been differing perceptions that we’ve seen as to how the ceasefire and – but, Ambassador Gor, I’d like to ask you about the defense partnerships.  And how far is Washington prepared to go for joint production, technology transfer, and, of course, developing advanced weapon systems?

AMBASSADOR GOR:  Well, look, I mean, that has existed already in India and it continues to exist.  And I think it’s important for your viewers to understand Lockheed is here, Boeing is here; co-production is happening.  So, jobs in the United States and jobs in India are progressing hand in hand on these production systems.

Our defense cooperation is at an all-time high.  I would say, I mean, you go just by the numbers and it is unmatched.  In the last month alone, we had 500 U.S. Army soldiers here training at Yudh Abhyas.  We had Tarang Shakti, the first time ever F-35s have been in India and participated in a joint exercise with Indians.  Our F-35s don’t go to any nation.  They go to nations we trust.  They go to partners we trust.  India is a very valuable partner to us in the Quad.  The Secretary has had multiple meetings at his level – including, by the way, next week another one.  So next week at the G20 in Atlanta, Dr. Jaishankar will be there, the Australians will be there, the Japanese will be there.  We’re also working towards a meeting between the leaders, including President Trump and Prime Minister Modi, in the next month. 

So, there’s a lot happening in the Quad.  Defense goes hand in hand with the United States, and India is a valued partner in that.  So, there’s a lot happening on that front. 

QUESTION:  I’m glad you mentioned the Quad, because how do you see, Secretary, the Quad evolving, particularly in the face of China’s growing assertiveness?  And what more can India and the United States do together to secure critical supply chains and reduce their dependence on China?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, just on the Quad point, it’s a relationship and it’s a construct that we’ve – it’s actually the first meeting I ever did as Secretary of State. 

QUESTION:  That’s right.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  It was a Quad meeting.  I think we’ve had more Quad meetings in the last year and a half than probably the first – the previous four years combined, at the foreign ministry level.  And I understand that, and we’re going to have a leader-level meeting now very shortly, probably in December at some point, and we’ll try to arrange even more before the end of President Trump’s term.  He still has two and a half years left. 

So, this is a very important relationship, but I think it’s important not just because we have four countries that are coordinating with one another.  We’re beginning to see outcomes.  We’re beginning to see results.  As an example, maritime awareness – the ability to know what’s happening under the water, threatening cables and so forth.  This is something that the Quad is working together on, and real things are happening. 

I think the same is true – I think it’s an area of cooperation that we can have when it comes to supply chains writ large.  The one thing I think is a consistent theme across the world, but certainly in the U.S.-India relationship, is we do not want to be overly dependent on any country in the world.  I’m not singling out China.  I’m saying any country in the world.  We don’t want to depend on any single country in the world for 90 percent of anything that’s critical to our economies.  And we have to have the domestic capacity to do certain things for ourselves.  I think that’s an interest India has.  That’s certainly an interest the United States has under President Trump.  And I think that’s something we can work together on.  And that is, what are those – where can we create domestic capabilities in a mutually beneficial way for both countries on various key sectors, be it artificial intelligence or technology or biomedicine or pharmaceuticals?  I mean, the list goes on and on – critical minerals, obviously everybody talks about those.

QUESTION:  And that’s why I want to come to you, Ambassador.  You’ve been instrumental in – for India joining the Pax Silica; I think as soon as you took over, we joined that.  Can India expect major American investments and technology partnerships that would help India become a key hub in terms of these strategic supply chains? 

AMBASSADOR GOR:  Well, I think it’s a great partnership.  India was one of the first 10 countries that the United States invited to join Pax Silica.  It’s because we trust India.  They’re a valued partner in the supply chain.  It is the reason that the Secretary was here twice in one year.  I am determined to bring the highest levels of our government here so they can talk to the highest levels of your government here and identify those opportunities.

As you know, in three weeks we have the Attorney General coming here to work with the folks in Delhi.  We’re going to have a counternarcotics conference in Delhi.  We’re bringing our DEA Administrator.  We’re bringing U.S. Attorneys.  We’ll bringing all sorts of individuals at the highest level.  To me it is important to have the highest levels of our government engaged with individuals here in India.

QUESTION:  Shifting gears a bit, Secretary Rubio, you had talked of America being in the process of being that – in being – stabilizing itself, right?  And in that context, shouldn’t it be welcoming highly skilled Indian professionals, as in the past, rather than hiking the prices for their work visas and also for Indian students coming to the U.S.?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, but that’s – no, but that’s a change in our immigration laws and it’s not one that’s built on India.  It’s not one that’s focused on India.  It happens to impact Indians that want to come to the United States and work, and there are businesses who are trying to bring in, but it’s not geared towards India.  It is global.  In fact, there is no meeting in the world that I do that doesn’t – they don’t raise some visa issue.

The United States has had a broken immigration system.  We’ve had a system in which – maybe not in this program but in others we had 20 million people unlawfully enter the country across our border.  We’ve had business-related immigration programs that in many cases have been rampant for fraud and abuse and have been misused in ways that have not made sense.  We have tensions in our own society.  I mean, what country in the world’s people would not react if they see that some of the best jobs in the country are being taken from people that are coming from abroad?

So, these things have to be addressed, and we’re trying to address them, but they’re not aimed at India.  They apply to any country, all – every country in the world.  That’s true on trade.  That’s true on immigration.  I know that for countries that are perhaps disproportionately impacted by a policy change in the United States it may feel like it’s being targeted, but it’s not.  It’s we’re going to get it right and we’re going to have a system that works for our economy and for the American people.

In the end, I will say this:  I expect that the Government of India will always put the people of India first and that you will always put the national interest of India first.  But I also hope everyone understands the United States under President Trump is going to put our people first, our workers first, and our country first.  And where I think friends can work together is when there are differences on this, our existing – our common interests, our longstanding relationship, and our shared values will allow us to work through some of those differences to reach outcomes that are positive for both countries. 

QUESTION:  Would you like to add anything?

AMBASSADOR GOR:  No, I mean, look, the Secretary is 100 percent right.  It’s – when we talk about America First, it doesn’t mean America alone.  And to the Secretary’s point, all these items that have changed that have impacted India, it’s not just India.  It’s the whole world.  The United States needed to take a look.  For too long we had open borders.  For too long people were coming into the United States and taking advantage of us.  We had leaders on both sides of the political aisle that did not look out for the American people.  That changed under President Trump.  That doesn’t mean it’s targeting any individual country.  We needed a reset.  The prime minister has been very clear here: India first.  There’s nothing wrong with that.  He should be looking out for his own country.  But people shouldn’t be surprised that our leadership is looking out for ours.

QUESTION:  Secretary Rubio, turning to geopolitics, President Putin said yesterday that Russia was willing for a tripartite meeting with the U.S. and Ukraine over ending the war.  What do you see as a realistic path to ending the Russia-Ukraine conflict?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, it’s a very difficult conflict, and I know the President has dedicated a tremendous amount of time to it.  We have people that do nothing all day but work on trying to find a way to make a difference and bridge those differences.  I would just say to you that that war – people keep talking about it’s a war in Ukraine.  That war is about Donbas.  It’s about one region of the country.  It’s – at its core, it’s about 11 percent of one part of that country that Russia wants and cannot take militarily and that Ukraine is unwilling to give up.  And they have good reasons why they don’t want to do that – for sovereignty and their own security long term.

And so the question is whether there’s some accommodation, that both sides will have to make some concessions in order to bring an end to the war.  This war is not going to be solved militarily.  This war is only going to end diplomatically.  And the question is: Can you arrive at an outcome in which both sides receive something of benefit but also give concessions and bring this to an end?

So, it’s been difficult, but I can tell you this: As hard as it is, it is impossible to do unless both sides are at the table talking, and we’re happy to play the mediating role in that regard.  So that’s really what we’re trying to do – not claiming that just getting them in the room is going to solve this problem, but we have no chance to solve it if we can’t get them in the room.

QUESTION:  And finally, winding up, Ambassador Gor, you’ve worked very closely with President Trump.  What’s the secret of working successfully with the President?

AMBASSADOR GOR:  I mean, look, the President is an incredible individual.  I have known the President for many years.  He is very direct.  He expects results.  And so the President is results-driven in a similar way, by the way, that your prime minister is.  He wants to move fast, and he wants to get things done.  And so to me, that has been something that, frankly, I have admired about our President.  Not every global leader is results-driven.  A lot of people love having these press conferences and meetings after meetings after meetings.  Our President wants results.  He wants them done now.

QUESTION:  And is the equation with Prime Minister Modi?

AMBASSADOR GOR:  Look, I’ve talked about this quite often.  They’re dear friends.  They’re dear friends and it works well because of that, because they see eye-to-eye on moving the ball forward, on getting things done, on delivering, right?  And so he holds the prime minister in the highest regard.  They’ve known each other for many years.  They’ll continue to engage.  They’ve had multiple phone calls in this month alone, right?  And so a lot happens behind the scenes that people are not aware of, but the two leaders are constantly in contact.

QUESTION:  And Secretary Rubio, what’s your experience of working with your boss, President Trump?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, he’s an historic figure.  There’s no doubt about it.  I think he’s provided for the presidency because of – he’s not an orthodox political figure.  He’s not a politician at all.  He’s a man of business whose entire life has been based on making decisions on the basis of what makes sense.

But here’s something else he doesn’t get credit for.  He’s visionary.  He imagines what people say is impossible.  He thinks things that people say, oh, we can’t do it because that’s never been done before, and then he achieves it and then he does it, when you look at issue after issue what the President has pushed towards and has been able to achieve that people didn’t think was possible because a traditional political figure would have never done it. 

So, I think it’s – for those of us who work for him and with him, it’s – it gives us energy to know that we have the ability to do things that you would not be able to do under someone who came from a traditional political background.  And I think in the case of foreign policy and in the world and in the realm of global affairs, it’s a very exciting time to be doing it. 

QUESTION:  And any – yes.

AMBASSADOR GOR:  Raj, I’ll add to that.  Remember this.  In the future people will look back on these years, and our President will be one of the greatest but also historical figures who achieved a lot.  We see it happening in real time now.  In the future when people reflect on his four years, on these four years of the White House, you will see things that have been unmatched.

QUESTION:  Now, speaking of a successor, Secretary Rubio, are you going to be in the presidential ballot in 2028?  (Laughter.)

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, I’m going to give you the same answer I’ve given American media.  I’m just not talking about that anymore.  I’ve already given multiple statements in regards to that.  You’ve only asked – this is the first time you’ve ever asked me because it’s the first time I’ve ever done an interview with you, but I’m plenty focused.  I have two jobs right now and they both take up all my time and energy, and I’m very happy doing those jobs.

QUESTION:  All right.  Secretary Rubio and Ambassador Gor, thank you very, very much for this interview today.  Thank you.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Thank you.

AMBASSADOR GOR:  Thank you, Raj.
